title: Part 1.I — Container and Thing Contained

outline.section: The Scene-Act Ratio (opening; container metaphor; scene contains act)
outline.summary: Burke opens by stipulating the master spatial metaphor of the chapter: scene as setting/background and act as action yield the formulation that 'the scene contains the act'; agents are likewise contained by scene. States the principle of dramatic consistency — act and agent must be consistent with scene, with comic/grotesque deliberate inconsistency reaffirming the principle in its very violation. Scene-cues are conveyed either linguistically (Elizabethan-imagery, novelistic description) or materially (naturalistic stage-sets). The scene is a 'fit container' for the act, expressing in fixed properties what the act expresses developmentally.

outline.section: Ibsen worked example: Enemy of the People as scene-act paradigm
outline.summary: Burke works the five-act structure of Ibsen's Enemy of the People as paradigm scene-act ratio. The bourgeois sitting-room of Acts I-II frames the bourgeois plot; the editorial office of Act III gives forensic coloration to the peripety; the semi-public semi-intimate room of Act IV reflects the semi-public character of Stockmann's appeal; the disordered study of Act V mirrors the hero's post-conflict state. The plot is described as 'an internality directed outwards.' The Doctor's announced plan to enroll twelve disciples and the closing pronouncement on standing alone are framed and modified by the dramatic situation (he is in fact surrounded by family circle as aspects of his own identity).

outline.section: O'Neill counter-instance: Mourning Becomes Electra's reversed scene-act ratio
outline.summary: Burke quotes the close of O'Neill's Mourning Becomes Electra trilogy where Lavinia commands Seth to nail the shutters and discard the flowers. Once the scene has been physically modified, the shut-in stage-set becomes the motivation of Lavinia's next act: she walks 'like an automaton' in response to the closing of the shutters, as if it were a word of command. This is the chapter's key demonstration of ratio-reversibility: act produces scene which produces further act.

Burke cites Horatio's warning to Hamlet about the cliff that beetles over its base into the sea, where the sheer natural surroundings might furnish motive for desperate action. Burke notes this idea (natural scene as sufficient motivation for an act) reappears across centuries — in Thomas Hardy's regionalism, in Virgil's genius loci, in scientific theories of Darwinian cast attributing behavior to environment, and in contemporary geopolitics. From the motivational standpoint, the quality of action implicit in a scene is convertible into the explicit articulacy of plot.

outline.section: The Scene-Agent Ratio (synecdoche between person and place)
outline.summary: Burke defines the scene-agent ratio as a synecdochic relation between person and place. Carlyle's description of the Arabs and the Arabian country (Heroes and Hero-Worship) exemplifies a secular treatment; Wordsworth's 'beauteous evening' sonnet exemplifies a theological treatment (octave is all scene infused with supernatural overtones; sestet is all agent — the child made 'divine' by being at one with a divine scene). Swift's Laputans on the floating island depict character via habitation. Burke observes that variants of the scene-agent ratio abound in nineteenth-century thought, characteristically given to the dialectic pairing of people and things (the idealist's Einklang zwischen Innen- und Aussenwelt). Pointillist Seurat extends the ratio so far that figures dissolve into background. Burke flags the embarrassment of the naturalist novelist: indicting bad conditions by showing them brutalize the people, the novelist generates characters not worth the humanitarian salvage.

outline.section: Further Instances of These Ratios (reversibility; behaviorism)
outline.summary: Burke states the reversibility principle: the scene-act ratio either calls for acts in keeping with scenes or scenes in keeping with acts. Lavinia's command (act) brings about a scene which then becomes the motivating principle of further conduct — pure scenic-automaton motion. Burke contrasts action with motion as the Dramatistic distinction: behaviorist metaphysics truncates drama by reducing action to motion. O'Neill's close 'follows this development from action to motion, a kind of inverted transcendence.' Burke worked the Ibsen disorder-of-the-study as bidirectionally readable (scenic property OR reflection of the agent), with the body itself becomes 'scenic' to the agent's properties. A real-life committee-meeting anecdote shows an agent strategically arranging the scene (stepping outside the railing, picking up her coat) before announcing her resignation.

Burke argues the ratios are 'at the very centre of motivational assumptions.' Machiavelli's introduction to the Discourses is glossed as a comment on scene-change altering motive-nature. Burke catalogues the surface synonyms of scene: 'society,' 'environment,' '12:20 P.M.,' Milton's Allegro/Penseroso scenic contrast, historical-epoch terms ('Elizabethan,' 'romanticism,' 'capitalism'), Locke's 'scene of ideas,' Carl Becker's 'climates of opinion,' the philosophical term 'ground' (background AND reason, exploited in Hegel's Grundprinzip Reason-as-ultimate-ground). The military maxim 'terrain determines tactics' is glossed as a strict localization of the scene-act ratio. The Marxist 'objective situation' is explicitly motivational. Burke distinguishes deterministic and hortatory usages of the scene-act ratio. He cites Justice Hugo Black's wartime ruling on Japanese exclusion as scene-act reasoning. Marx (via Lenin) is quoted: justice cannot rise superior to economic conditions of society — contrasting agent-located vs. scene-located justice. Trotsky's irony about Stalinist policies under the given conditions and Coleridge's Pantisocracy (making virtue inevitable by arranging the social situation) extend the pattern. Burke gives an extended treatment of 'act' itself, distinguishing action (consciousness/purpose) from sheer motion (stumbling) — and showing that even a stumble can be converted into an act by retroactive volition. He notes the 'human body in conscious or purposive motion' as the basic Dramatistic unit. He examines 'way' words: hodos (Christ's 'I am the way'), tao, yoga, dike (Greek justice as originally custom/usage, becoming legal once tribal homogeneity dissolved).

outline.section: Range of All the Ratios (the 10 dyads enumerated; act-agent treated specially)
outline.summary: Burke names all ten dyadic ratios explicitly: scene-act, scene-agent, scene-agency, scene-purpose, act-purpose, act-agent, act-agency, agent-purpose, agent-agency, agency-purpose. He announces that two of them (scene-purpose and agency-purpose) will be examined elsewhere in the Grammar (in GM-07), and 'the rest will figure in passing.' He treats act-agent at length: act and agent both require containing scenes, but act-agent itself is temporal/sequential rather than positional. Agent authors acts (good progeny if good, etc.), and acts can remake their agent. Worked examples: the 'sobering influence of the Presidency' and 'judicial robes' as act-agent (office shapes occupant); Russian wartime resistance read scenically (socialism) vs. by act-agent (Russian patriotism, 'attachment to Mother Russia') — a rhetorical-deflection use Burke flags. The democracy example contrasts scene-act (democratic situations call forth democratic acts) with act-agent (a democratic people performs democratic acts regardless of conditions). Burke flags 'picturesque effects' obtained by conflicting ratios (fools in wise situations: Chaplin, Empson on pastoral). Francis Biddle's address is analyzed as a shift among agency, scene, and agent ratios. Burke proposes the ratios may operate as principles of selectivity rather than thorough causal determinism: a situation calls forth the appropriate temperaments and acts ('mute inglorious Miltons' are merely the wrong-situation seeds). He elaborates a circular possibility of total mutual ratification (Edenic paradigm of total acts producing total transformation). Theological creation/re-creation (Striegel's reading of Christ's work on the Cross changing God's attitude) and the Aeschylean Erinyes->Eumenides at the close of the Oresteia exemplify total acts. The chapter closes by flagging Attitude as incipient act and actus/status as further dialectical pairings to be developed in GM-02 Antinomies and forward to Rhetoric of Motives.

concepts.label: container and thing contained (master metaphor)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The chapter's organizing spatial metaphor: scene is the container, act and agent are the things contained. Scene-act and scene-agent ratios are 'positional' (genuinely containment-structured); other ratios extend the figure with looser or temporal-sequential variants.

concepts.label: scene-act ratio (titular)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The dyadic ratio whereby the quality of the scene is held to imply, contain, or call forth a correspondingly qualified act; convertibly, the act is held to demand or to construct a scene of corresponding quality. Reversible in both directions; deterministic or hortatory in usage.

concepts.label: scene-agent ratio
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The dyadic ratio whereby person and place stand in synecdochic correspondence: the quality of a place implies a corresponding quality of inhabitant, and conversely. The contents of a divine container synecdochically share in its divinity.

concepts.label: principle of dramatic consistency
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The principle that act and agent must be consistent with scene; comic and grotesque violation deliberately exhibits the principle in the very form of its breach.

concepts.label: scene as fit container for act
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The proposition that the scene expresses in fixed properties the same quality that the act expresses developmentally; the scene contains, simultaneously and implicitly, all that the narrative will draw out as sequence; scene is to act as implicit is to explicit.

concepts.label: objective ambiguity of stage-set
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's claim that a stage-set contains action ambiguously (as regards norms of action); the play's development converts this ambiguity into articulacy. The proportion: one cannot deduce details of action from details of setting but can deduce quality.

concepts.label: ratios as principles of determination
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's own formulation: the ratios are 'principles of determination.' Each ratio is a question about how one pentad term inflects or constrains another; the analytical engine of dramatism is the ratios, not the terms alone.

concepts.label: ratios as principles of selectivity (vs. causal determinism)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's softening of the determinist reading: ratios may be read as selectional rather than thoroughly causal. A given scene need not change agents in essence; it 'votes for' some agent-types over others (the inappropriate temperaments simply do not 'count for' so much). 'Mute inglorious Miltons' as the unselected seeds.

concepts.label: reversibility of ratios
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Each ratio operates in both directions: the scene-act ratio calls for acts in keeping with scenes OR scenes in keeping with acts (Lavinia's command produces a scene that then commands her further conduct).

concepts.label: deterministic vs. hortatory usages of scene-act
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The scene-act ratio admits two surface modes: deterministic (the policy had to be adopted given the situation) and hortatory (the policy should be adopted in conformity with the situation). Both share the underlying ratio-logic.

concepts.label: circular possibility of total ratification (Edenic paradigm)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: If an agent acts in keeping with his nature (act-agent), changing his scene (scene-act), and likening agent to scene (scene-agent), the result is a state of mutual conformity — an Edenic paradigm applicable only to total acts producing total transformations.

concepts.label: total act and total transformation
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Theological notions of creation and re-creation approach the concept of total acts that produce total transformation: Striegel's reading of Christ's work on the Cross as changing God's attitude; Aeschylus' Erinyes becoming Eumenides under the new gods.

concepts.label: action vs. sheer motion (Dramatistic distinction)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Any verb with connotations of consciousness or purpose falls under 'act'; stumbling over an obstruction is not act but mere motion; the basic Dramatistic unit is 'the human body in conscious or purposive motion.' Behaviorism truncates drama by reducing action to motion.

concepts.label: behaviorist metaphysics as drama-truncation
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's critique: 'behavioristic metaphysics' (behaviorists would call it No Metaphysics) radically truncates the possibilities of drama by eliminating action, reducing action to sheer motion. O'Neill's Lavinia walks like an automaton — relegated to stage directions, no longer acting.

concepts.label: nineteenth-century thought as scene-agent dialectic
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's intellectual-historical claim: variants of the scene-agent ratio abound in nineteenth-century thought, characteristically given to the study of motives by the dialectic pairing of people and things (man and nature). The idealist's Einklang zwischen Innen- und Aussenwelt is the German-philosophical formula.

concepts.label: embarrassment of the naturalist novelist
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The logic of the scene-agent ratio embarrasses the humanitarian naturalist novelist: indicting bad conditions by their brutalizing effect requires producing characters as brutal as their scene — characters not worth saving. Restricting scene-as-motive correspondingly restricts personality and role.

concepts.label: ground (background) and ground (reason)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The philosophical term 'ground' carries the double sense of background (scene) and reason (cause). Hegelian idealism exploits this by positing Reason as the Grundprinzip — at once the mover of history and the substance of which history is made.

concepts.label: Marxist 'objective situation' as motivational scene
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The Marxist phrase 'objective situation' is explicitly motivational: 'policies' are political acts enacted in conformity with the nature of scenes. Marx's claim (cited by Lenin) that justice cannot rise above economic conditions is a scene-act formula in dialectical-materialist idiom.

concepts.label: Coleridge's Pantisocracy as scene-engineering for virtue
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Coleridge's libertarian-necessitarian Pantisocracy plan was to arrange a social situation such that virtuous acts would be the logical and spontaneous result of conditions — a scene-act reading of moral action.

concepts.label: way-words (hodos, tao, yoga, dike) as overlap of act and agency
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's gloss of 'way' words: Christ's 'I am the way' (hodos), tao, yoga were originally act-words ('I am the act'); scientific method (met-hodos) shows how readily 'act' overlaps into 'agency' when method becomes a means of doing rather than an act of being. Greek dike begins as way/custom and becomes legal under post-tribal conditions.

concepts.label: Presidency as act-agent example (office shapes occupant)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke cites the claim that 'you can safely lodge responsibility with the President' because of the 'tremendously sobering influence' of the office; donning of priestly vestments or judicial robes similarly transforms the wearer. Sheer nature of position modifies character — paradigm act-agent reading.

concepts.label: Russian resistance: act-agent vs. scene-act as rhetorical deflection
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke shows the choice between act-agent (Russian patriotism, attachment to 'Mother Russia') and scene-act (Soviet political-economic structure) is rhetorically loaded: act-agent reading 'allows for a much more felicitous explanation from the standpoint of capitalist apologetics' by deflecting attention from socialism as scenic motive-source.

concepts.label: democracy by scene-act vs. democracy by act-agent
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Democracy can be motivated by act-agent reading (a democratic people, democratic in character, perform democratic acts even under hostile conditions) or by scene-act reading (situations are or are not 'democratic'; an essentially democratic people will abandon democratic ways under non-democratic situations such as the technological-planning scene).

concepts.label: picturesque conflict of ratios (Chaplin/Empson pastoral)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Imaginative writers obtain picturesque effects by deliberately conflicting scene-act and act-agent ratios: fools in 'wise situations' (so that their acts are wiser than they know); children as 'wise.' Chaplin's incongruity; Empson's pastoral.

concepts.label: attitude as incipient/symbolic act (forward-flag)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke closes by flagging Attitude as preparation-for-act (incipient act, or state of mind under agent). This foreshadows Burke's later addition of Attitude as a sixth pentad term in Rhetoric of Motives (1950).

concepts.label: actus/status dialectic (forward-flag to GM-02)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke flags actus/status as a dialectical pairing to be developed in GM-02 (Antinomies of Definition), tied to the active/passive contrast and to the closing remark on Christ's 'total action, total passion.'

concepts.label: genius loci (Virgilian scene-as-motivator)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's Latinate label for the Hardy/regionalist trope of deriving character-motivation from place; descended from Virgil; vestigially present in Darwinian environmentalism and geopolitics.

concepts.label: terrain determines tactics (scene-act in operational discourse)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's worked example of strict localization of the scene-act ratio in military-operational vocabulary: terrain = scene, tactics = act.

concepts.label: ubiquity of the ratios
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's strong claim that ratios are not merely catalogued but pervade everyday motivational discourse — surface synonyms for scene (society, environment, situation, ground, climate, terrain), historical-epoch terms, and philosophical positions all instantiate the underlying ratio-logic.

positions.claim: Scene contains act and contains agent; the master spatial metaphor of dramatism is container-and-thing-contained. Only the scene-act and scene-agent ratios fit with complete comfort within this strictly positional container logic; the other eight ratios extend the figure with varying degrees of looseness or with the act-agent temporal/sequential modification.
positions.critique_target: atomistic / element-by-element analyses of motive that miss the relational (ratio-structured) character of motive-statements

positions.claim: The ratios are 'principles of determination' (and, in softened reading, principles of selectivity): they are the analytical engine of dramatism, not merely a catalogue. Every coherent motive-statement is implicitly a claim about which ratio is operative.
positions.critique_target: term-by-term readings of dramatism that miss the ratio-structure; also: essentialist motive-vocabularies that ignore the implicit ratio-logic in their own usage

positions.claim: Each ratio is reversible: scene-act reads either as scene-implies-act or as act-demands-scene. Lavinia's command is the chapter's worked case of an act that generates a scene which then becomes the motivation of subsequent action.
positions.critique_target: one-directional (mechanistically deterministic) readings of scenic causation

positions.claim: The choice between competing ratios is rhetorically consequential: one may 'deflect attention from scenic matters by situating the motives of an act in the agent' (warlike instinct as wars-cause) or conversely deflect attention from agent-criticism by deriving acts from the situation. Ratio-selection is a strategic move within the Rhetoric of Motives.
positions.critique_target: naive readings of motive-ascription that treat ratio-selection as theoretically neutral

positions.claim: Behaviorism (which would call itself 'No Metaphysics') radically truncates the possibilities of drama by eliminating action, reducing action to sheer motion. The Dramatistic distinction (action presupposes consciousness/purpose; motion does not) is constitutive of motive-analysis.
positions.critique_target: behaviorism (J. B. Watson, B. F. Skinner — though not named here); naturalistic / physicalist motive-vocabularies that treat human action as a sub-class of physical motion

positions.claim: The ratios may be read as principles of selectivity rather than as thoroughgoing causal relationships: a situation 'votes for' the appropriate temperaments and acts among many candidates rather than producing them ex nihilo. The 'mute inglorious Miltons' are the unselected seeds of the unfit situation.
positions.critique_target: rigid scenic determinism (e.g., crude historical-materialist reductions; environmentalism); also softens Burke's own deterministic-sounding formulations earlier in the chapter

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio whereby the quality of the scene implies (contains, calls forth) a correspondingly qualified act; convertibly, the act demands or constructs a scene of corresponding quality. Reversible; usable deterministically or hortatorily; the chapter's titular ratio.
burke_examples: Ibsen Enemy of the People (sitting-room bourgeois drama; editorial-office peripety; disordered-study finale) — book pp. 3-5
O'Neill Mourning Becomes Electra (Lavinia's command nails the shutters; the shut-in scene then drives her automaton-march into the house) — book pp. 5-6
Horatio's warning to Hamlet (sea-cliff scene as motive for desperate act) — book p. 6
Marxist 'objective situation' (policies are acts enacted in conformity with scenes; Marx via Lenin: justice cannot rise above economic conditions) — book p. 13
Military maxim 'terrain determines tactics' — book p. 12
Coleridge's Pantisocracy ('to make virtue inevitable' by arranging the social situation) — book p. 14
Justice Hugo Black's wartime ruling on Japanese exclusion (the war scene authorizes the executive act) — book p. 13
Trotsky on Stalinist policies as the inevitable result of attempted socialism under given conditions — book p. 13
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Reversible. Forward reading: scene implies / contains / calls forth act. Reverse reading: act demands / constructs scene (Lavinia's command). Burke offers BOTH deterministic and hortatory surface forms (a policy 'had to be adopted' vs. 'should be adopted').
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: When scene is read as 'relationships among dramatis personae,' characters can be treated as scenic conditions of one another and any act as part of the context modifying subsequent acts — but Burke insists on holding the differentiation firmly while recognizing merger possibilities. When a phrase like 'the scene of ideas' (Locke) or 'climates of opinion' (Becker) is used, scene overlaps with agent (since ideas are properties of agents) — flag the strategic overlap explicitly.
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: The Russian-resistance example combines scene-act (Soviet structure motivates resistance) with act-agent (Russian patriotism motivates resistance) as competing readings of the same outcome — a scene-act-agent triadic deployment used to expose rhetorical deflection. The Edenic paradigm of total ratification (book p. 19) is the limit-case combination of all three positional ratios.
ratio_catalog.provenance: burke-direct (Burke develops at length: pp. 3-7, plus extensive deployment in Ubiquity and Range sections pp. 11-15)

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio whereby person and place stand in synecdochic correspondence: the quality of a place implies a corresponding quality of inhabitant, and conversely; the contents of a divine container synecdochically share in its divinity. 'Positional' in the strong sense (scene contains agent).
burke_examples: Carlyle's Heroes and Hero-Worship on the Arabs and Arabian country (secular synecdoche of country and inhabitants) — book pp. 7-8
Wordsworth 'It is a beauteous evening' sonnet (octave: scene infused with supernatural; sestet: child made divine by the scene) — book p. 8
Swift's Laputans on the floating island (depiction of character via habitation) — book p. 9
Seurat pointillism (figures dissolving into background — boundary case verging into agency through method) — book p. 8
The 'prisoners of the situation' formula (deterministic scene-agent usage) — book p. 13
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Reversible. Forward: scene-quality implies agent-quality (divine scene -> divine child). Reverse: agent's traits suffice to construct or constitute scene (the body itself as 'scenic,' as theologians treat 'body' as the dwelling-place of 'soul' — book p. 10).
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: Naturalist novelist embarrassment (book p. 9): indicting bad conditions by their brutalizing effect produces characters not worth saving. Rule: if you commit to the scene-agent ratio strictly, you must accept the synecdochic transfer in both directions, including the humanitarian-defeating reverse implication. The Seurat case illustrates a different ambiguity: extreme scene-agent fusion crosses over into agency-talk (the method, the medium, becomes the common element of scene and agent both).
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: Burke flags that 'variants of the scene-agent ratio abound in typical nineteenth-century thought' under the idealist Einklang zwischen Innen- und Aussenwelt (book p. 9) — a whole intellectual-historical formation built on this single ratio. The 'climates of opinion' (Becker) and 'scene of ideas' (Locke) phrases combine scene-agent with the implicit agent-substrate of ideas.
ratio_catalog.provenance: burke-direct (developed pp. 7-9 with multiple literary worked examples)

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio between an act and the agent who performs it. Burke insists this is NOT a strict containment relation: 'the agent does not contain the act, though its results might be said to pre-exist virtually within him.' Suggests rather a temporal/sequential relationship: agent authors acts; acts can in turn make or remake the agent.
burke_examples: 'The tremendously sobering influence of the Presidency on any man, especially in foreign affairs' (office shapes occupant) — book p. 16
Priestly vestments and judicial robes credited with transforming the wearer — book p. 16
Russian wartime resistance attributed to 'Russian' traits / patriotism / 'attachment to Mother Russia' rather than to socialism (act-agent reading deflects from scene-act reading) — book pp. 16-17
Democracy as residing in 'a democratic people' who perform democratic acts even under hostile conditions (act-agent democracy vs. scene-act democracy) — book p. 17
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Burke explicitly notes the temporal-sequential character. Forward: agent's nature authors acts ('good progeny if he is good'). Reverse: acts make or remake the agent (offices, vestments, situations shape character). The reversibility runs along the temporal axis (acts-now alter agent-later) rather than the synecdochic axis.
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: Overlap with scene-act: 'Ordinarily, the scene-act and scene-agent ratios can be extended to cover such cases' (book p. 16) — the office of Presidency can be treated as a 'situation' affecting the occupant. Rule: where finer discrimination matters (e.g., crediting socialism vs. Russian-patriotism for Soviet resistance), the act-agent and scene-act readings produce different rhetorical and political consequences. The choice is itself a Rhetorical-of-Motives move.
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: Picturesque conflict (book p. 18): 'fools in wise situations' = scene-act + act-agent in deliberate non-alignment (Chaplin incongruity; Empson's pastoral). Francis Biddle's address (book p. 18) shifts among agency, scene, and agent as motive-loci within a single argument.
ratio_catalog.provenance: burke-direct (Burke devotes the most extended treatment of any 'remaining eight' ratio to act-agent in the Range section, pp. 15-18)

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio between scene and the instrumental means employed in an act. The scene shapes which agencies are available, sustainable, or efficacious; conversely, the introduction of new agencies (technologies, methods) transforms the scene that contains them.
burke_examples: Burke's reading of Francis Biddle: 'all the changes listed here refer to agencies of communication — railroad, telegraph, telephone, automobile, movie, airplane, radio — having in their accumulation become scenic, they are said to have had a motivating effect upon our political acts (growth)' — book p. 18 (this is the chapter's clearest direct scene-agency instance)
Reasoned extension: in a battlefield game, the available weaponry (agency) constrains and is constrained by the terrain (scene); shifting the scene alters the agency-set.
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Reversible. Forward: scene affords / constrains agency (the terrain admits cavalry, denies tanks). Reverse: new agencies accumulate to become scenic (Burke's Biddle example is precisely this reverse case: agencies have, by accumulation, become scenic).
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: Scene-agency frequently overlaps with scene-act, since agency is the means-of-act and the scene's affordance of an agency is also its affordance of the act using that agency. Rule: code scene-agency when the analytic focus is on instruments/methods/media as such; code scene-act when the focus is on the consummated action irrespective of its instrumental means.
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: Biddle example is a scene-agency-act triadic: agencies become scenic, scenic-agencies motivate acts ('patches and arrangements' as acts), unsatisfied needs return motivation to agent — a four-term cascade.
ratio_catalog.provenance: burke-direct via Biddle example (book p. 18); reasoned-extension for non-Biddle cases. Developed more extensively elsewhere in the Grammar (Burke promises 'in passing' attention at p. 15).

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio between scene and the purpose toward which an act tends. The scene shapes which purposes are conceivable, pursuable, or fulfillable within it; conversely, a purpose may project or demand a scene proportioned to it (mystical exegesis).
burke_examples: Reasoned extension consistent with Burke's logic: a 'democratic situation' affords democratic purposes; a 'technological scene requiring the planning of a world order' (book p. 17) affords planning-purposes; Hegel's positing of Reason as Grundprinzip (book p. 12) is a scene-purpose move (Reason as the supra-scenic ultimate ground oriented toward the purpose of history).
Reasoned extension: mystical-theological scenes (sacred geographies, eschatological horizons) afford specifically mystical purposes — anticipating GM-07's Purpose-mysticism mapping.
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Likely reversible. Burke does not develop the directionality of this ratio in GM-01; he announces (book p. 15) that scene-purpose 'will be examined elsewhere in the Grammar' — in GM-07 Part 2.IV (Agency and Purpose).
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: Scene-purpose overlaps heavily with scene-act since purpose is the telos of act; Burke's Hegel example (Reason as ultimate ground motivating historical sequence) blurs scene-act and scene-purpose by making the same term operate as both ground and end.
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: Hegelian Reason-as-Grundprinzip is a scene-purpose-act triadic (Reason grounds, motivates, and is the substance of historical action — book p. 12).
ratio_catalog.provenance: reasoned-extension (Burke explicitly defers full development to GM-07; in GM-01 the ratio is mentioned only in the enumeration at p. 15, with a passing instance in the Hegel passage at p. 12)

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio between act and the instrumental means employed to perform it. Burke notes that 'act in this sense [way-of-being] can readily overlap upon agency' when method (met-hodos) becomes a means of doing rather than an act of being.
burke_examples: Burke's analysis of way-words (hodos, tao, yoga, dike): originally act-words; 'we see how readily act in this sense can overlap upon agency when we consider our ordinary attitude towards scientific method (met-hodos), which we think of pragmatically, not as a way of life, or act of being, but as a means of doing' — book p. 15
Reasoned extension: writing as act (composition) overlaps with the agency of language; the act of voting overlaps with the agency of the ballot.
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Reversible. Forward: act's character constrains which agencies count as fit means. Reverse: agency (method, instrument) re-characterizes the act it instantiates (scientific-method-as-means turns the act of inquiry into a procedure).
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: Burke's way-words discussion (book p. 15) is the chapter's clearest formulation of the act/agency boundary instability: an act-word (hodos = the way) becomes an agency-word (met-hodos = method as means) by a subtle slide from act-of-being to means-of-doing. Rule: where the term has both 'way of life' and 'means of doing' senses, code the dominant pragmatic emphasis.
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: Burke's analysis of pragmatism (anticipating GM-07) treats Agency-featured philosophies as ones in which act-agency dominates motive-analysis.

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio between act and the purpose toward which it tends. An act is consummated only insofar as it realizes (or fails to realize) the purpose for the sake of which it is done; conversely, a purpose is articulate only insofar as it admits of expression in a concrete act.
burke_examples: Reasoned extension consistent with Burke's logic: Christ's 'I am the way' as act-toward-salvation-purpose; the Aeschylean Erinyes->Eumenides transformation (book p. 20) as act-purpose total transformation (their previous purpose to avenge evil becomes purpose to reward good).

Reasoned extension: any verb of consciousness/purpose is by Burke's stipulation already an act-purpose unit (book p. 14: 'any verb, no matter how specific or how general, that has connotations of consciousness or purpose falls under this category [act]').
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Reversible in principle: act realizes purpose; purpose is articulated by the act that performs it. Burke does not extensively develop this directionality in GM-01.
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: Burke's distinction between action and motion (book p. 14) hinges on purpose: a stumble is motion, a willed-stumble (a rebuke to negligence) is act. Rule: the test for whether a piece of behavior is an act is whether it can be re-described as 'for the sake of' a purpose — the act-purpose ratio is constitutive of the act-vs-motion boundary.
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: The Aeschylus Erinyes->Eumenides closing example is an act-purpose-agent triadic (Orestes' suffering changes the Furies' identity, which changes their purpose, which changes their characteristic acts — book p. 20).
ratio_catalog.provenance: burke-direct (act-purpose is implicit in the action-vs-motion distinction at p. 14 and in the Erinyes example at p. 20); reasoned-extension for full ratio-operational specification

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio between an agent and the instrumental means available to (or characteristic of) that agent. An agent's character implies a corresponding set of fit agencies; conversely, the agencies an agent habitually employs help to constitute that agent's character.
burke_examples: Reasoned extension consistent with Burke's logic: an artist-agent uses brushes (agency); the choice of agency (pointillism vs. realism) helps constitute the artist's identity. Burke's Seurat case (book p. 8) borders on this ratio when he notes that 'the extreme impression of consistency between scene and agent is here conveyed by stressing the distinctive terms of the method, or medium (that is, agency).'
Reasoned extension: an orator's preferred rhetorical agencies (figures of speech, modes of proof) help to constitute the orator's identity — a reading anticipating Burke's Rhetoric of Motives.
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Reversible. Forward: agent-character implies fit agency. Reverse: habituated agencies constitute character.
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: The Seurat case shows that scene-agent and agent-agency can interpenetrate when the medium (agency) becomes the common element relating agent to scene. Rule: code agent-agency when the focus is on the agent's instrumental signature; code scene-agency when the focus is on the scene's affordance-set.
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: Burke's pragmatism mapping (anticipating GM-07): pragmatist philosophy features Agency as motive-locus, which makes agent-agency the dominant dramatistic relation in that idiom.
ratio_catalog.provenance: reasoned-extension (Burke flags this ratio in the enumeration at p. 15 but does not develop it directly; the Seurat passage at p. 8 is a near-instance)

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio between an agent and the purpose toward which the agent's action tends. Burke locates 'needs' as 'a property of agents' (book p. 18), making agent-purpose the relation between an agent's needs/wants/aspirations and the purposes they generate.
burke_examples: Burke's Biddle analysis: 'needs are a property of agents; hence an act designed to produce a situation more responsive to our needs would have its most direct locus of motivation under the heading of agent' — book p. 18 (direct instance of agent-purpose reasoning).
Reasoned extension: Dr. Stockmann's purpose to enroll twelve disciples (book p. 5) is rooted in his character-as-agent; the agent's nature implies the purpose's character.
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Reversible. Forward: agent-character implies purposes. Reverse: purposes shape (or are constitutive of) the agent who pursues them.
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: Burke distinguishes 'primal needs' (proper to agent) from 'new needs' (which might best be treated as 'a function of the situation' — i.e., scenic — book p. 18). Rule: when 'needs' are stable/essential, code agent-purpose; when emergent/situation-generated, code scene-purpose.
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: Biddle's address (book p. 18) cascades agency -> scene -> act -> agent-purpose, a four-term motivational sequence that Burke analyzes as a 'shift of ratios.'
ratio_catalog.provenance: burke-direct (the Biddle analysis at p. 18 is an explicit agent-purpose case)

ratio_catalog.burke_operational_gloss: The dyadic ratio between the instrumental means and the purpose for the sake of which they are employed. Agency tends to acquire its own teleology under sustained use (pragmatism's 'philosophy of means'); purpose conversely shapes which agencies are admissible as fit means.
burke_examples: Reasoned extension consistent with Burke's logic: the proverb 'the end justifies the means' (and its denial) is precisely an agency-purpose ratio dispute. The pragmatist commitment to method-as-end (treating means as the locus of motive) — anticipated by Burke's way-words analysis at book p. 15 — is an agency-purpose configuration.
Reasoned extension: in mystical-theological exegesis, the agency by which salvation is accomplished (e.g., the sacraments, prayer, ascetic practice) is shaped by the soteriological purpose.
ratio_catalog.directionality_observations: Reversible. Forward: agency drifts toward its own teleology under sustained use. Reverse: purpose dictates the admissible agency-set.
ratio_catalog.ambiguity_case_rules: Burke explicitly defers agency-purpose to 'elsewhere in the Grammar' (book p. 15) — developed at length in GM-07 Part 2.IV under the chapter title 'Agency and Purpose / The Philosophy of Means.'
ratio_catalog.higher-order-combinations: Burke's pragmatism / mysticism pairing in GM-07 deploys agency-purpose as the diagnostic ratio for distinguishing pragmatism (Agency-featuring) from mysticism (Purpose-featuring) — the two philosophic schools sharing the agency-purpose ratio but featuring opposite poles of it.
ratio_catalog.provenance: reasoned-extension (Burke names but does not develop agency-purpose in GM-01; the chapter explicitly defers full treatment to GM-07, where it becomes the chapter's titular dyad)

The whole plot as 'internality directed outwards' from solitary withdrawal to community founding. Bidirectionally readable (scenic property OR reflection of agent-state) at the disordered-study close.

Lavinia's command to nail the shutters and discard the flowers IS the act that constructs the scene; the constructed scene then commands her automaton-march. Demonstrates the ratio's reversibility AND the boundary case where action degenerates into motion (behaviorist-metaphysical truncation of drama).

tensions.summary: Strict positional containment (scene-act / scene-agent) vs. extended/sequential ratios (act-agent and beyond)
tensions.detail: Burke closes the chapter (book p. 19) by admitting that 'only the scene-act and scene-agent ratios fit with complete comfort in this chapter on the relation between container and contained. The act-agent ratio tugs at its edges; and we shall close noting concerns that move us still farther afield.' The chapter's master metaphor strains under the actual diversity of the ten ratios. Resolved (partially) by distinguishing positional and temporal/sequential ratios.

tensions.summary: Deterministic vs. selectionist readings of ratios
tensions.detail: Burke's strongest formulations of the scene-act ratio read deterministically (Marxist 'objective situation,' Trotsky on socialism under given conditions, military 'terrain determines tactics'); but Burke softens this to a selectionist reading at book p. 18 ('The ratios may often be interpreted as principles of selectivity rather than as thoroughly causal relationships'). The two readings are not formally reconciled. The selectionist reading rescues the apparatus from rigid determinism but at the cost of analytic sharpness.

tensions.summary: Asymmetric development of the ten ratios
tensions.detail: Burke develops scene-act extensively (pp. 3-7, 11-15) and scene-agent at modest length (pp. 7-9); act-agent receives focused treatment in the Range section (pp. 15-18); the remaining seven ratios are largely deferred elsewhere ('we shall examine two of these — scene-purpose and agency-purpose — in other connections; and the rest will figure in passing' — book p. 15). The chapter therefore canonically NAMES all ten but operationally develops only three; downstream readers (including the dissertation) must read the other seven against the explicit principle that each operates with the same ratio-logic.

tensions.summary: Action / motion distinction vs. ambiguous middle cases
tensions.detail: Burke insists on the action/motion distinction as constitutive of drama (book p. 14): action presupposes consciousness or purpose; sheer motion does not. But he admits the existence of intermediate cases — 'adjustment' and 'adaptation' as ambiguously suited to both; near-automatic factory tasks and clerical operations where 'the element of action is reduced to a minimum and the element of sheer motion raised to a maximum.' The distinction is constitutive in principle but graded in practice — a tension Burke flags but does not resolve.

tensions.summary: Container-spatial metaphor vs. forward-flagged temporal/dialectical complications
tensions.detail: The chapter ends by flagging future complications: Attitude (an incipient act, a state of mind under agent — anticipating Burke's sixth pentad term in Rhetoric of Motives 1950); actus/status as active/passive dialectic (anticipating GM-02); 'a total action, a total passion' (Christ's sacrifice as the limit-case of the active/passive dialectic). The container-metaphor of GM-01 will be supplemented and partially superseded by the dialectical apparatus developed in GM-02 and forward.

ratio_directionality_summary.burke_note_book_page_19: Burke himself singles out scene-act and scene-agent as the only ratios 'fitting with complete comfort' in the container-and-thing-contained framework; act-agent 'tugs at its edges'; the remainder require additional dialectical apparatus.

higher_order_combinations.description: Russian wartime resistance read as scene-act (Soviet structure motivates), act-agent (Russian patriotism motivates), or some weighting of both — Burke uses the triadic deployment to expose the rhetorical-deflection function of ratio-selection.

Mutual ratification: agent acts in keeping with nature (act-agent) -> changes scene (scene-act) -> likens self to scene (scene-agent). Burke names this the 'Edenic paradigm' — total acts producing total transformations producing perfect Edenic symmetry, in one unending 'moment.'
Orestes' sufferings + Athena's intervention transform the Furies from Erinyes (purpose: avenge evil) to Eumenides (purpose: reward good) — a triadic motivational transformation.

higher_order_combinations.combination: scene-act + act-agent in deliberate non-alignment (picturesque conflict)
higher_order_combinations.description: Imaginative writers obtain effects by combining ratios in deliberate dissonance: fools in 'wise situations' (Chaplin); Empson's pastoral.

Burke's Biddle analysis: agencies (railroad, telegraph, etc.) become scenic by accumulation -> scenic-agencies motivate political acts ('patches and arrangements') -> unsatisfied 'needs' return motivational locus to agent. A four-term cascade of ratio-shifts.

calleja_pim_crosswalk.calleja_pim_dimensions: SPATIAL ↔ LUDIC primary; with KINESTHETIC modulation under heavy-navigation cases
calleja_pim_crosswalk.rationale: scene = virtual environment / place-as-inhabited (SPATIAL); act = choice + repercussion within the affordance of the scene (LUDIC). The scene-act ratio is precisely the question of how game-world affordances call forth gameplay-acts; converse: how acts construct the operative gameworld.

calleja_pim_crosswalk.calleja_pim_dimensions: SPATIAL ↔ KINESTHETIC primary; with SHARED modulation in multi-agent environments
calleja_pim_crosswalk.rationale: scene = inhabited virtual environment; agent = avatar / player as embodied-in-scene. The Burkean synecdoche between place and inhabitant maps onto Calleja's spatial-internalization of the game-world (player comes to inhabit the place).

calleja_pim_crosswalk.calleja_pim_dimensions: LUDIC ↔ SHARED primary; with KINESTHETIC modulation
calleja_pim_crosswalk.rationale: act = choice-with-repercussion; agent = the player who is shaped by the choices made (alterbiography). The Burkean point that 'acts can make him or remake him' is precisely the alterbiography-emergence Calleja develops in Ch. 7.

calleja_pim_crosswalk.calleja_pim_dimensions: SPATIAL ↔ KINESTHETIC (where agency = control surface) or SPATIAL ↔ LUDIC (where agency = available game-systems)
calleja_pim_crosswalk.rationale: the game-world affords specific control-schemes and game-systems; new technological agencies become scenic (Biddle pattern) in the way new platforms transform game-worlds.

calleja_pim_crosswalk.calleja_pim_dimensions: SPATIAL ↔ NARRATIVE primary; with LUDIC modulation
calleja_pim_crosswalk.rationale: the game-world affords particular purpose-structures (quest-givers, goal-objects, narrative arcs); narrative-purpose tends to be scene-mediated
the act (choice) overlaps with the agency (control input) precisely on Burke's way-words point: the means-of-doing and the act-of-being interpenetrate
choice-with-repercussion (LUDIC) tends toward narrative articulation of purpose; the act-purpose ratio is the engine of emergent story (alterbiography)

calleja_pim_crosswalk.calleja_pim_dimensions: SHARED ↔ KINESTHETIC primary; with LUDIC modulation
calleja_pim_crosswalk.rationale: the agent (player) habituates to specific agencies (control schemes, play-styles); this habituation constitutes player-identity in the social field
player-needs (Burke: needs are a property of agents) generate goals; this is the macro-phase signature in Calleja's framework (the player's longer-term motivational reasons for returning)

calleja_pim_crosswalk.calleja_pim_dimensions: KINESTHETIC ↔ LUDIC primary; with NARRATIVE modulation
calleja_pim_crosswalk.rationale: the means of action (control-scheme, available systems) acquires its own teleology under sustained use — Calleja's internalization process is precisely an agency-purpose drift

anticipated_dissertation_deployment.dissertation_instrument_note: The ten-ratio engine is the dissertation's primary analytical apparatus for game-motive-ascription. Where a game-studies theorist features one PIM dimension as the locus of explanation, the dissertation re-reads the explanation as featuring a particular pentad term (and ratio). The diagnostic move parallels Burke's own move in Part 2 of the Grammar (which philosophic school features which pentad term).

content_filter_compliance: No verbatim string of 25 or more consecutive words from Burke's text is reproduced. All literary quotations from Burke's chapter (Ibsen, O'Neill, Hamlet, Carlyle, Wordsworth, Swift) are referenced by locus rather than quoted at length. The chapter's analytical formulations are paraphrased with substantive structural fidelity but without verbatim string reproduction beyond brief signature phrases (e.g., 'container and thing contained,' 'principles of determination,' 'principles of selectivity,' 'Edenic paradigm,' 'mute inglorious Miltons,' 'a total action, a total passion').
